items.followUp: Differentiate between aerobic and anaerobic respiration. State the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the processes by their oxygen requirement.
rubric.description: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen, whereas anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting the oxygen requirements.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the extent of glucose breakdown.
rubric.description: Aerobic respiration completely breaks down glucose; anaerobic respiration breaks it down incompletely.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting complete and incomplete breakdown.

rubric.why: Contrasts the products and relative energy yield of the two processes.
rubric.description: Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water and releases more energy; anaerobic respiration releases less energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast of products and energy yield.

rubric.why: Explains anaerobic respiration and states its site.
rubric.description: Anaerobic respiration is the incomplete breakdown of glucose without oxygen in the cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing glucose breakdown without oxygen and identifying the cytoplasm.

rubric.why: Gives a correct example of anaerobic respiration and its product.
rubric.description: In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; in muscle cells, it produces lactic acid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct example with its product or products.

modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen, whereas anaerobic respiration takes place without oxygen.
Aerobic respiration completely breaks down glucose; anaerobic respiration breaks it down incompletely.
Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water and releases more energy; anaerobic respiration releases less energy.
Anaerobic respiration is the incomplete breakdown of glucose without oxygen in the cytoplasm.
In yeast it produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; in muscle cells it produces lactic acid.

items.followUp: Name the three types of muscle tissue and state where each is found.

rubric.why: Describes the defining property and function of muscle tissue.
rubric.description: Muscle tissue consists of cells that contract and produce movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that muscle cells contract to produce movement.

rubric.why: Identifies skeletal muscle and its control.
rubric.description: Skeletal or striated muscle is voluntary.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming skeletal or striated muscle and identifying it as voluntary.

rubric.why: Identifies smooth muscle and its control.
rubric.description: Smooth or non-striated muscle is involuntary.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming smooth or non-striated muscle and identifying it as involuntary.

rubric.why: Identifies cardiac muscle, its control, and its location.
rubric.description: Cardiac muscle is involuntary and is found in the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying cardiac muscle as involuntary and stating that it is found in the heart.

modelAnswer: Muscle tissue is made of cells that contract and produce movement.
Skeletal or striated muscle is usually attached to bones and is voluntary.
Smooth or non-striated muscle is found in the walls of internal organs and is involuntary.
Cardiac muscle is found in the heart and is involuntary.

items.followUp: Why is a control group included in a scientific experiment?

rubric.why: Defines the control group by contrasting its treatment with that of the experimental group.
rubric.description: The control group is kept under the same conditions as the experimental group but does not receive the factor being tested.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the control group is kept under comparable conditions and does not receive the tested factor.

rubric.why: Explains the purpose of the control group.
rubric.description: It provides a standard for comparison so that the effect of the tested factor can be identified.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that comparison with the control group helps identify the effect of the tested factor.

modelAnswer: A control group is kept under the same conditions as the experimental group but does not receive the factor being tested.
It provides a standard for comparison so that the effect of the tested factor can be identified.
